from one upper story to another, from one cave to another, from one shelter to another, or from one hut to another.
He goes from one hut to another; he goes from one gabled chamber to another; he goes from one watchtower to another;
he goes from one upper story to another; he goes from one turret to another; he goes from one assembly hall to another;
he goes from one pavilion to another; he goes from one foot of a tree to another.
Or else he goes to where the monks are sitting; there he becomes the companion of one, or the third of two, or the fourth of three.
There he indulges in much idle chatter, namely:
talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food.
Talk about drinks, talk about clothes, talk about vehicles, talk about beds, talk about garlands, talk about scents, talk about relatives, talk about villages,
talk about towns, talk about cities, talk about countries, talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about wells,
talk about those who have departed in the past, talk about various matters, talk about speculation concerning the world, and talk about speculation concerning the ocean.
Or [engaging] in talk about existence and non-existence. In this way too, one is fidgety with the feet.
"Not fidgety with the feet" means...
One should abandon fidgeting with the feet, dispel it, bring it to an end, and lead it to non-existence;
one should be detached from fidgeting with the feet, abstain from it, refrain from it, have emerged from it, escaped it, and be liberated and dissociated from it.
One should dwell, move, wander, conduct oneself, behave, protect, preserve, and maintain oneself with a mind that has transcended all boundaries, delighting in seclusion.
One who delights in seclusion, is devoted to internal mental tranquility, does not neglect meditative absorption,
is endowed with insight, frequents empty dwellings, is a meditator, delights in meditation, is devoted to unity, and values the ultimate goal—
such a meditator is not one who dangles his feet.
"Abstain from remorse; do not be negligent.
Remorse means: remorse regarding the hands, remorse regarding the feet, and remorse regarding both hands and feet;
perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, perceiving what is allowable as unallowable, and perceiving the improper time as the proper time.
Perceiving what is timely as untimely, perceiving what is blameless as blameworthy, and perceiving what is blameworthy as blameless; whatever such worry, state of worrying,
act of worrying, mental remorse, or mental scruple there is—
this is called worry (*kukkucca*).
Moreover, remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise for two reasons: on account of what has been done and on account of what has not been done.
How do remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise on account of what has been done and what has not been done?
“‘I have committed misconduct of body, I have failed to perform good conduct of body’—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
‘I have committed misconduct of speech, I have failed to perform good conduct of speech’—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
‘I have committed misconduct of mind, I have failed to perform good conduct of mind’ … [and so on].”
“‘I have committed the taking of life; I have failed to abstain from the taking of life’—thus arises remorse … mental distress.
‘I have committed the taking of what is not given … I have committed sexual misconduct …’”
I have committed false speech;
I have committed divisive speech;
I have committed harsh speech.
Idle chatter has been committed by me… covetousness has been committed by me… ill will has been committed by me…
“Wrong view has been done by me; right view has not been done by me”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
In this way, remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise from what has been done and what has not been done.
Or else, “I have not fulfilled my duties regarding the moral precepts”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
“I am one who does not guard the doors of the sense faculties,” … “I am one who lacks moderation in eating,” … “I am one who is not devoted to wakefulness.”
“I am not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension,” … “the four foundations of mindfulness have not been developed by me,” … “the four right strivings have not been developed by me,” …
“I have not developed the four bases of psychic power,” … “I have not developed the five faculties,” … “I have not developed the five powers,” …
“I have not developed the seven factors of awakening,” … “I have not developed the noble eightfold path,” … “Suffering has not been fully understood by me. …
“Origination has not been abandoned by me,” ...
“the path has not been developed by me,” ...
“cessation has not been realized by me”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
"Abstain from worry": one should abstain from worry, desist from it, refrain from it; one should abandon worry, dispel it, make an end of it, bring it to non-existence.

One should be one who has turned away from worry, desisted from it, refrained from it, gone out from it, escaped from it, and fully liberated; one should dwell with a mind that has transcended its limits—this is "abstain from worry."

“Let him not be negligent” means: let him be one who acts with care, one who acts with persistence, one who acts with steadfastness, one whose conduct is not indolent, one whose desire is not cast aside, one whose burden is not cast aside—namely, heedfulness regarding wholesome states.
[He reflects: “When shall I fulfill the aggregate of virtue that is unfulfilled, or when shall I support with wisdom here and there the aggregate of virtue that is already fulfilled?”

Whatever zeal, effort, exertion, ardor, fortitude, and indefatigability there is therein; whatever mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving, determination, application, and heedfulness there is regarding wholesome states:
"When shall I fulfill the aggregate of concentration...
[and so on] ...the aggregate of wisdom?"

the aggregate of liberation … the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation … ‘When shall I fully understand suffering that has not been fully understood, abandon the defilements that have not been abandoned, develop the path that has not been developed, and realize cessation that has not been realized?’”

Whatever zeal, effort, exertion, ardor, fortitude, and unyielding persistence there is therein, as well as mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving, determination, application, and heedfulness regarding wholesome states—
one should abstain from remorse and not be negligent. Then,
a bhikkhu should dwell in lodgings that are quiet and secluded.
Now, regarding the euphonic combination of words (*padasandhi*)... [etc.
...a seat is that on which one sits:
a bed, a bench, a mattress, a mat, a piece of hide, a grass-strewing, a leaf-strewing, or a straw-strewing.
"Lying down" refers to lodgings: a dwelling, a gabled house, a mansion, a cell, or a cave—it is among such seats and beds.
"A bhikkhu should dwell in places that are quiet."

“In lodgings that are quiet, noiseless, free from the sound of people, secluded from human habitation, and suitable for retreat— one should walk, wander, dwell, move about, conduct oneself, protect oneself, sustain oneself, and maintain oneself”—
thus a bhikkhu should dwell in those seats and couches that are quiet.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
The meditator should not fidget with his feet;
he should abstain from remorse and not be negligent;
likewise regarding seats and beds—
“A bhikkhu should dwell among those who are quiet.
One should not indulge in sleep;
one should be ardent and devote oneself to wakefulness.
One should abandon dancing, singing, laughter, play,
sexual intercourse, and adornment.
One should not indulge excessively in sleep.
Having divided the night and day into six parts, one should spend five parts in wakefulness and lie down for one part;
thus, one should not indulge in sleep.
One should devote oneself to wakefulness, ardent and resolute.
Here, a bhikkhu should purify his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the day;
he should purify his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the first watch of the night;
during the middle watch of the night, he should lie down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other.

Mindful and clearly comprehending, having directed his attention to the perception of rising, he should, upon arising during the last watch of the night, purify his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
"He should devote himself to wakefulness" means: he should devote himself to wakefulness, cultivate it, practice it, pursue it, habituate himself to it, and repeatedly practice it.
One should devote oneself to wakefulness.
"Ardent" means that "ardor" is said to be energy (*vīriya*).
That which is mental energy— exertion, endeavor, striving, effort, perseverance, fortitude, steadfastness, firmness, unrelenting endeavor,
non-abandonment of desire, non-abandonment of the burden, grasping of the burden,
energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and right effort.
One who is endowed with this ardor, fully endowed, approached, fully approached, attained, fully attained, and possessed of it, is called "ardent.
Thus, being ardent, one should devote oneself to wakefulness.
One should abandon sloth, deceit, laughter, play, sexual intercourse, and adornment.
Laziness (*tandi*) is sloth, the state of being slothful, the condition of having become slothful; it is indolence, the state of being indolent, the condition of having become indolent.
Deceit (*māyā*) is said to be a deceptive mode of conduct.
Herein, someone, having engaged in misconduct with the body...
Having engaged in misconduct by way of speech ... [and] by way of mind, one forms an evil wish for the sake of concealing it:
"May they not know me," he wishes; "May they not know me," he intends; "May they not know me," he speaks such words; "May they not know me," he exerts himself with the body.

That which is such deceit, transgression, cheating, crookedness, hypocrisy, evasion, concealment, total concealment, hiding, total hiding, covering up, total covering up, non-disclosure, non-revelation, shielding,
and the performance of evil deeds— this is called *māyā*. Here, someone laughs excessively, laughing with bared teeth.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“This, bhikkhus, is childish in the discipline of the Noble Ones, namely, laughing with bared teeth for too long.
Play: there are two kinds of play—
There is bodily play and verbal play.
What is bodily play?
They play with elephants, they play with horses, they play with chariots, they play with bows, and they play with dice.
They play; they play with ten-pieces, they play in the air, they play on the path of circumambulation,
they play with *santikā*, they play with *khalikā*, they play with *ghaṭikā*, they play with counting-slips in the hand,
they play with dice, they play with mud-cloths, they play with *vaṅkaka*, they play with *mokkhacikā*, and they play with spinning tops.
They play; they play with hand-sticks, they play with toy-carts, they play with bows,
they play with letter-games, they play with mind-games, they play with mimicry—
this is physical sport.
What is verbal play?

Making sounds with the mouth such as *mukhabherika*, *mukhālambara*, *mukhaḍiṇḍimaka*, *mukhavalimaka*, *mukhabheruḷaka*, *mukhadaddarika*; acting, chatter, singing, and frivolous behavior—this is verbal play.

The "act of sexual intercourse" refers to that which is contrary to the true Dhamma, the village custom, the practice of the low-born, the censurable, the water-adjacent, the secret, the mutual attainment of two by two.
For what reason is it called the act of sexual intercourse?

Because it is the common practice of two who are lustful, inflamed with passion, impure, obsessed, and whose minds are overwhelmed; because it is the shared nature of these two equals—for that reason it is called the act of sexual intercourse.
Just as two quarrelsome people are called "a pair of lovers," two who cause brawls...
two who cause disputes... two who cause legal issues... two who cause contention... two who are disputants... two who engage in debate are called "a pair of lovers";

even so, because it is a common practice for both who are lustful, inflamed, lecherous, obsessed, and whose minds are overwhelmed—being equal in this regard—it is therefore called "the act of sexual intercourse."
Adornment: there are two kinds of adornment—there is the adornment of the householder, and there is the adornment of the one who has gone forth.
What is the adornment of the householder?
Hair and beard, garlands, perfumes, ointments, ornaments, jewelry, clothing, bedding and seats,
turbans, anointing, rubbing, bathing, massaging, mirrors, collyrium, floral wreaths and unguents,
facial powder, facial paste, handbands, topknots, quivers, and swords.
An umbrella, variegated sandals, a turban, a jewel, a yak-tail fan, and white garments with long fringes—
this is the adornment of a householder.
What is the adornment of one who has gone forth?

Adorning one’s robes, adorning one’s bowl, adorning one’s lodging, or the adorning, beautifying, playing with, sporting with, grasping at, state of being gripped by, fickleness, and restlessness regarding this putrid body or external requisites—
this is the adornment of one who has gone forth.
One should abandon sloth, deceit, laughter, play, sexual intercourse, and adornment.

"One should abandon, dispel, bring to an end, and lead to non-existence languor, deceit, laughter, playfulness, and sexual intercourse, together with adornment, together with its retinue, together with its equipment"—
thus one should abandon languor, deceit, laughter, playfulness, and sexual intercourse along with adornment. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One should not indulge in sleep,
but should devote oneself to wakefulness with ardor;
one should abandon sloth, deceit, laughter, and play.”
One should abandon sexual intercourse along with adornments.
One should not practice the Atharva-veda, nor interpret dreams or bodily marks, nor even astrology.
My follower should not practice incantations, the production of fetuses, medical treatments,
nor should he engage in sorcery, dream interpretation, physiognomy, or astrology.
The practitioners of *āthabbaṇa* employ *āthabbaṇa* spells; when a city is besieged or a battle has arisen, they incite calamity among the enemy armies, adversaries, and foes;
they incite misfortune, they incite disease, they cause paralysis, they cause piercing pain, they cause cholera, and they cause dysentery.
Thus do the fortune-tellers employ their arts of divination.
Dream-interpreters explain dreams: "If one sees a dream in the morning, such is its result;
if one sees a dream at midday, such is its result."
For one who sees a dream in the evening time, such is the ripening;
for one [who sees it] in the first watch...
for one [who sees it] in the middle watch... [the ripening is likewise].
He who lies on his right side during the last watch of the night...
he who lies on his left side... he who lies on his left side...
He who lies on his back… he who lies face down… he who sees the moon…
He who sees the sun … he who sees the great ocean … he who sees Sineru, the king of mountains …
He who sees an elephant...
he who sees a horse...
he who sees a chariot...
He who sees an army array... he who sees a delightful grove...
he who sees a pleasant park...
For one who sees the beauty of the forest...
for one who sees the beauty of the land...
for one who sees the beauty of the lotus pond, such is the ripening of the result.
In this way, dream-interpreters declare the meaning of dreams;
mark-readers declare the meaning of marks—
the mark of a gem, the mark of a staff, the mark of a cloth, the mark of a sword, the mark of a spear, and the mark of a bow.

The characteristics of weapons, the characteristics of women, the characteristics of men, the characteristics of girls, the characteristics of boys, the characteristics of female slaves, the characteristics of male slaves,
the characteristics of elephants, the characteristics of horses, the characteristics of rhinoceroses, the characteristics of bulls, the characteristics of oxen,
the characteristics of goats, the characteristics of rams, the characteristics of roosters, the characteristics of snakes, and the characteristics of lizards.
"The mark of the pericarp, the mark of the tortoise, the mark of the deer"— thus do the readers of marks explain the marks.
The readers of constellations explain the constellations.
There are twenty-eight lunar mansions.
With this mansion, the entry into a house should be performed; with this mansion, the crown should be bound on;
with this mansion, the marriage ceremony should be conducted; with this mansion, the bringing of the fan should be performed; with this—
"One should go on a journey according to the lunar mansion.
Thus do the readers of the stars indicate the lunar mansion.
They practice the Atharva-veda, dream interpretation, and the science of marks, and they also calculate the lunar mansions.

One should not practice, nor engage in, nor follow, nor adopt and live by means of fortune-telling (*āthabbaṇa*), dream-interpretation (*supina*), physiognomy (*lakkhaṇa*), and astrology (*nakkhatta*).
Or rather: one should not take them up, nor learn them, nor bear them in mind, nor reflect upon them, nor examine them, nor apply them—this is "fortune-telling, dream-interpretation, and physiognomy;
and also astrology, one should not practice."
"My follower should not practice the art of making fetuses miscarry or the art of curing [diseases].
"Viruta" refers to the science of falconry (*migavākka*).
Those who teach falconry explain the science of falconry as follows:
They claim to know the cries and calls of birds or quadrupeds.
Thus do those who recite the *migavākka* texts proclaim the *migavākka*.
Those who administer means for conception bring about pregnancy.
For two reasons the embryo does not become established:
either because of microorganisms or because of a disturbance of the bodily humors (vāta).
She gives medicine for the sake of warding off those microorganisms or that disturbance of the humors.
In this way, those who cause conception bring about conception.
There are five types of medical treatment:
surgery with instruments, treatment for arrow wounds, internal medicine, exorcism, and pediatrics.

One who is devoted to me (*māmaka*) is one who is devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha; such a person either cherishes the Blessed One as "mine," or the Blessed One accepts that individual as his own.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Those monks, bhikkhus, who are hypocritical, stubborn, talkative, sycophantic, arrogant, and unconcentrated—they are not mine, bhikkhus."
“Those monks are mine, yet those monks, bhikkhus, have departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya;
those monks do not attain growth, increase, or abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
But those monks, bhikkhus, who are free from deceit, free from chatter, wise, steadfast, and well-composed—they indeed are mine.”

“Monks, those monks who are mine have not departed; those monks, monks, have not gone away from this Dhamma and Vinaya, and those monks attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
[But] those who are hypocritical, stubborn, talkative, and arrogant—”
Those who are haughty and unconcentrated do not grow in the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Those who are unassuming, free from guile, wise,
undeluded, and well-composed—
verily they cause the Dhamma to grow.
“Taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

My follower should not practice, nor resort to, nor cultivate, nor indulge in, nor engage in, nor follow, nor adopt and persist in, either abortifacients, virilifics, or medical treatments. He should not practice them, nor resort to them, nor cultivate them, nor indulge in them, nor engage in them, nor follow them, nor adopt and persist in them.

Or alternatively: "He would not take it up, would not learn it, would not bear it in mind, would not attend to it, would not mark it, and would not apply himself"—a follower of mine would not practice the cry, the means of inducing conception, or the medical treatment.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One should not practice fortune-telling, dream interpretation,
or physiognomy, nor astrology; nor should one engage in the interpretation of animal cries or the performance of rites for inducing pregnancy.”
“My follower should not practice medicine.
A bhikkhu should not be shaken by blame, nor should he be uplifted when praised.
One should cast out greed together with stinginess,
anger, and slander; one should not tremble at blame.
In this case, some monks revile, disparage, or reproach others on account of their birth,
clan, lineage, physical beauty, wealth, Vedic study, occupation, craft, field of knowledge,
learning, eloquence, or for some other reason; being thus reviled...

When reviled, censured, and blamed—with reproach, condemnation, disparagement, defamation, and the destruction of reputation—he would not tremble, he would not tremble greatly, he would not tremble all over;
he would not be afraid, he would not be terrified, he would not be utterly terrified;
he would not fear, nor fall into panic. He would be fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread.
"One should dwell with the hair on one's body stilled" means one should not be shaken by blame.
"A bhikkhu should not be elated when praised."
In this case, some monks praise others on account of birth, or clan, or noble lineage, or beauty of complexion,
or wealth, or Vedic study, or field of occupation, or craft, or branch of science,
or learning, or eloquence, or by some other such basis; they praise, extol, laud, and eulogize them.
When praised, lauded, celebrated, and extolled— with praise, with laudation, with celebration,
and with eulogy— one should not become uplifted, one should not become elated, one should not give rise to conceit, one should not become stiff; one should not generate conceit because of that,
nor be made rigid or arrogant by it, thinking, "I am held in high esteem."
"A praised bhikkhu should not be puffed up;
he should dispel greed along with stinginess, as well as anger and slander.

"Greed" (*lobha*) means that which is greed, the act of being greedy, the state of being greedy; it is lust, the act of lusting, the state of lusting; it is covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Stinginess" refers to the five kinds of stinginess:
stinginess regarding dwelling, [stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gain, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma]... grasping is called stinginess.
Anger is that which is resentment, repulsion, hostility, and opposition of the mind;
it is wrath, fury, and intense fury; malice, corruption, and intense corruption; the perversion of the mind, mental corruption; anger, being angry, the state of being angry;
malice, being malicious, the state of being malicious; perversion, being perverse, the state of being perverse; opposition and hostility.
Harshness is a lack of gentleness, a state of displeasure in the mind.

Slander means that here someone is a speaker of malicious words; having heard something here, he reports it there for the sake of dividing these people, or having heard something there, he reports it here for the sake of dividing those people.

Thus, he is one who divides those who are united, or who incites those who are divided; he delights in factions, rejoices in factions, finds pleasure in factions, and speaks words that create factions.
This is called malicious speech.
Moreover, one instigates malicious speech for two reasons:
either out of a desire for favor or with the intention of causing division.
How does one employ malicious talebearing out of a desire for affection?

Thinking, "I will become dear to him, I will become pleasing to him, I will become trustworthy, I will become an intimate, I will become well-disposed toward him," one thus employs malicious talebearing out of a desire for affection.
How does one instigate malicious talebearing with the intention of causing division? One thinks:

"May these people become divided, may they be separated, may they be at variance, may they be split, may they be alienated, may they fall into two factions; may they break apart and not come together, and may they dwell in suffering and lack of comfort.
In this way, one instigates malicious talebearing with the intention of causing division.

"One should dispel greed along with stinginess, and anger and slander"—this means one should push away, drive out, abandon, eliminate, bring to an end, and cause the non-existence of greed and stinginess, anger and slander; thus:
"one should dispel greed along with stinginess, and anger and slander."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“A bhikkhu should not be shaken by blame, nor should he be uplifted when praised.”
One should cast away greed along with stinginess,
and anger as well as slander;
one should not engage in buying and selling.
A bhikkhu should not utter reproach against anyone anywhere;
he should not become attached to the village,
nor should he flatter people out of a desire for gain.
"Regarding 'one should not stand by the buying and selling':
those acts of buying and selling that are prohibited in the Vinaya are not intended here in this context.
How does one stand by buying and selling?"
If one deceives five people by exchanging a bowl, a robe, or any other requisite for a profit or out of desire for gain,
one stands in buying and selling.
How does one not stand in buying and selling?
He does not exchange five things—whether a bowl, a robe, or any other requisite—with another for deception, nor does he do so hoping for profit.
In this way, he does not engage in buying and selling.
"He should not engage in buying and selling" means this.
"One should not stand in buying and selling, nor persist therein; one should abandon buying and selling, dispel it, bring it to an end, lead it to non-existence.
One should be aloof from buying and selling, abstain from it, refrain from it, have emerged from it, be detached from it, and be fully liberated;
one should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries"—thus it was said.
"One should not stand in the buying and selling of a body;
a bhikkhu should not utter reproach anywhere.
What are the defilements that constitute reproachers?
There are some ascetics and brahmins who possess supernormal power, have the divine eye, and are knowers of others' minds;
they see even from afar, yet those nearby do not see them, and they understand the mind with their own mind.

There are also deities who possess supernormal power, have the divine eye, and are knowers of others' minds; they see even from afar, yet those nearby do not see them, and they understand the mind with their own mind.
They might censure one on account of gross defilements, or middling defilements, or subtle defilements.
What are the gross defilements?
Bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.
These are called the gross defilements.
What are the intermediate defilements?
Sensual thought, ill-will thought, and cruelty thought.
These are called the intermediate defilements.
What are the subtle defilements?

Thoughts concerning relatives, thoughts concerning one’s native land, thoughts concerning immortality, thoughts associated with benevolence toward others, thoughts associated with gain, honor, and renown, and thoughts associated with not being treated with contempt.
These are called subtle defilements.
One should not revile them with gross defilements, nor with medium defilements, nor with subtle defilements;
one should not utter revilement, should not commit it, should not produce it, should not generate it, should not bring it about, and should not cause it to arise.
He would not give rise to them; he would abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence those defilements that cause reproach;
he would be detached, secluded, withdrawn, emerged, and liberated from those defilements that cause reproach, and he would dwell with a mind free from boundaries and completely released.
"Anywhere" means: anywhere at all, in anything whatsoever, whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally—a bhikkhu should not utter a reproach anywhere.
"And he should not be attached to the village."
How does one become attached to the village?

Here, a bhikkhu dwells in close association with householders in the village; he shares in their joys and sorrows, being happy when they are happy and suffering when they are suffering; and when there are duties or tasks that have arisen, he personally undertakes the effort to perform them.
In this way, too, one becomes attached to the village.
Alternatively, a bhikkhu, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe,
enters a village or town for alms with body unguarded, speech unguarded, mind unguarded, without established mindfulness,
and with the sense faculties unrestrained.
Thus, in this and that he becomes attached; in this and that he grasps; in this and that he is bound; in this and that he falls into ruin and disaster.
In this way, too, one is attached to the village.
How is one not attached to the village?

Here, a bhikkhu dwells in a village unassociated with householders; he does not share their joys, nor share their sorrows; he is not happy when they are happy, nor distressed when they are distressed; and when duties or tasks arise, he does not involve himself in them.
In this way, too, he is not attached to the village.
Or else, a bhikkhu, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, enters a village or town for alms.
He enters with body guarded, speech guarded, mind guarded, mindfulness established,
and sense faculties restrained. He does not cling here and there,
he does not grasp here and there, he is not bound here and there, and he does not fall into ruin and disaster here and there.
Thus too, one does not cling to the village.

"And one should not be attached to the village" means: one should not cling to the village, should not grasp it, should not be bound by it, should not be obstructed by it; one should be without greed, unattached, unmuddled, uninfatuated, free from longing, devoid of longing, having abandoned longing...
[as above] ...one should dwell with oneself become sublime.
One should not become attached to the village.
One should not chatter to people out of a desire for gain.
What is chattering?
For one who is dependent on gain, honor, and renown, who has evil desires, who is dominated by desire, who looks with the eye of worldly gain,
and who values worldly conditions— whatever addressing, talking, conversing, prattling, chatting, inciting,
instigating, coaxing, persuading, speaking what is not dear, flattering, bean-soupery, servility, and backbiting directed toward others;
Whatever there is of gentle speech, kindly speech, smooth speech, and non-harsh speech therein—
this is called "flattery.
Furthermore, one flatters people for two reasons:
Either placing oneself low and placing another high, one flatters people; or placing oneself high and placing another low, one flatters people.
How does one place oneself low and place another high while flattering people?
[One says: "You have been very helpful to me; depending on you, I obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
"Even those others who think they can give to me or do for me, it is by depending on you and regarding you that even my former name, derived from my mother and father, has vanished.
It is through you that I am known as 'the associate of such-and-such a family' or 'the associate of such-and-such a family.'"
Thus, by placing himself low and placing another high, he speaks to people.
How does he speak to people by placing himself high and placing another low?
“I have been of great benefit to you; it is because of me that you have gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma...”

She has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; she abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
I give you the recitation, I give you the opportunity for questioning, I explain the Uposatha, and I authorize the building work.
"But if you, having abandoned me, should honor, revere, esteem, and worship others"—
thus one speaks to people, exalting oneself and deprecating another.
One should not speak to people out of a desire for gain.
For the sake of gain, with gain as condition, for the cause of gain, for the production of gain, while maturing people for the sake of gain, one should not engage in flattery;
one should abandon flattery, dispel it, eliminate it, bring it to an end, and lead it to non-existence.

One should be aloof from flattery, abstain from it, refrain from it, have departed from it, be escaped from it, and be liberated from it; one should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries. Thus: [one should train].
One desiring gain should not engage in bartering with people.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"One should not stand in the trade of buying and selling."
“A bhikkhu should not utter reproach against anyone anywhere;
he should not become attached to a village,
nor should he flatter people out of a desire for gain.”
A bhikkhu should not be a woodcutter,
nor should he utter purposeless speech;
he should not practice insolence.
How should one not engage in contentious talk?
"And a monk should not be a disputant.
Here, a certain person is a disputant, one who boasts.
Thus he lauds himself and boasts: "I am endowed with virtue," or "endowed with vows," or "endowed with both virtue and vows";

or by birth, or clan, or noble lineage, or beauty of complexion, or wealth, or Vedic study, or field of occupation, or craft, or branch of science, or learning, or eloquence, or by some other such basis.

He vaunts himself, saying, "I have gone forth from a high-born family," or "I have gone forth from a family of great wealth," or "I have gone forth from a family of abundant wealth" ... [and so on] ...
or "I am a master of the Suttantas," or "I am an upholder of the Vinaya," or "I am an expounder of the Dhamma," or "I am a forest-dweller" ...
[and so on] ... or "I am an attainer of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Thus he vaunts himself and boasts.
Thus one should not speak, nor should one prattle; one should abandon speech, dispel it, make it vanish, bring it to non-existence.
One should be detached from prattling, abstinent, thoroughly abstinent, having emerged from it, having escaped it, and being fully liberated.
One should dwell with a mind that is dissociated and free from the boundaries [of such speech].
A monk should not be a quarrelsome person,
nor should he utter speech that is incited by others.
What is speech incited by others?
Here, someone speaks speech connected with robes, speaks speech connected with almsfood, speaks speech connected with lodgings, or speaks speech connected with requisites for the sick,
such as medicines and provisions— this too is called "speech prompted by attachment.
Or else, [it is speech] for the sake of robes, for the sake of almsfood, for the sake of lodgings, or for the sake of requisites for the sick, such as medicines and provisions.
He speaks truth and he speaks falsehood; he speaks maliciously and he speaks without malice;
he speaks harshly and he speaks without harshness; he speaks idle chatter and he speaks without idle chatter;
he also utters incantations.
This too is called speech that is prompted.
Or else, with a confident mind, one teaches the Dhamma to others, thinking:
"Oh, may they hear my Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, may they gain confidence; and being confident, may they show their confidence toward me."
This is called "premeditated speech.
"And one should not utter premeditated speech" means that one should not speak,
converse, or utter even a single word of Dhamma instruction that has been premeditated.
One should not utter it, one should not speak it; one should abandon such speech, dispel it, make it vanish, bring it to non-existence.

One should be aloof from such speech, abstain from it, refrain from it, have emerged from it, be detached from it, and be liberated from it, dwelling with a mind for which the boundaries [of such speech] have been removed. Thus...
One should not speak words that are ill-applied.
One should not train in insolence.
As for "insolence," there are three kinds of insolence:
Bodily insolence, verbal insolence, and mental insolence.
What is bodily insolence?
Here, someone displays bodily insolence even when in the presence of the Saṅgha, and displays bodily insolence even when in the presence of a group.
He displays physical immodesty in the dining hall; he displays physical immodesty in the sauna;
he displays physical immodesty at the bathing place; he displays physical immodesty even when entering among the houses;
and he displays physical immodesty even once he has entered among the houses.
How does one display physical impudence when gone into the Saṅgha?
Here, a certain person, having entered the Saṅgha, stands jostling the elder bhikkhus out of a lack of respect;
he sits jostling them; he stands in front of them; he sits in front of them; he sits on a high seat; or he sits with his head covered.
He sits down; he speaks while standing; he speaks while waving his arms about.
In this way, one displays bodily impudence when among the Saṅgha.
How does one display bodily impudence when among a group?
In this case, someone who has joined a group, out of a lack of respect for the elder bhikkhus, walks with sandals on while they are walking without sandals;
he walks on a high walkway while they are walking on a low walkway; he walks on a raised terrace while they are walking on the ground;
he stands in such a way as to jostle them, he sits in such a way as to jostle them, and he stands in front of them.
He sits in front [of others], he sits on a high seat, he even sits with his head covered;
he speaks while standing, and he speaks while waving his arms about.
In this way, having entered a group, he displays physical impudence.
How does one display physical impudence in the dining hall?
Here, someone, out of a lack of respect, sits encroaching upon senior bhikkhus;
he even obstructs junior bhikkhus from their seats; he stands jostling them, and he sits jostling them, even in front of them.
He stands [while others are seated], he sits even in front [of others], he sits on a high seat, he sits with his head covered,
he speaks while standing, and he speaks while waving his arms. In this way,
he displays physical impudence in the dining hall.
How does one display physical impudence in a sauna?
Here, someone in a sauna stands pushing elder bhikkhus because he lacks consideration;
he sits pushing them; he stands in front of them; he sits in front of them; he sits on a high seat; and he does so without asking permission.
He throws in firewood and closes the door even without asking permission.
In this way, he displays physical impudence in the sauna.
How does he display physical impudence at a bathing place?
In this case, someone might enter a bathing place with a lack of mindfulness, pushing against elder bhikkhus as they enter, or entering ahead of them;
pushing against them while bathing, or bathing ahead of them; bathing above them;
or pushing against them as they emerge, or emerging ahead of them, or emerging above them.
In this way, he demonstrates physical impudence at a water-crossing.
How does he demonstrate physical impudence when entering between houses?
Here, a certain person, when entering between houses, out of a lack of respect, walks brushing against elder bhikkhus, walks ahead of them, or even bypasses elder bhikkhus to walk in front of them.
In this way, one entering among the houses displays physical immodesty.
How does one who has entered among the houses display physical immodesty?
Here, a certain person, having entered among the houses, enters even when told, "Do not enter, venerable sir," or "Do not stand."
When told, "Venerable sir, stand," he stands; when told, "Venerable sir, do not sit," he sits;

he enters even where there is no designated place, he stands even where there is no designated place, and he sits even where there is no designated place—even in those private, secluded, and concealed rooms of families where women of the family, daughters of the family, daughters-in-law of the family, and young maidens of the family reside.
They sit down there, they enter abruptly, and they touch the head of a young boy.
Thus, having entered an inhabited house, one displays physical impudence—
this is physical impudence.
What is verbal insolence?

Here, someone displays verbal insolence even when in the midst of the Saṅgha, displays verbal insolence even when in the midst of a group, and displays verbal insolence even when entered among the houses of others.
How does one display verbal insolence when in the midst of the Saṅgha?

In this case, someone who has entered the Saṅgha, acting out of disrespect, speaks the Dhamma, answers questions, or recites the Pātimokkha to monks who have come to the monastery, either without having asked or requested the elders among the monks,
and he speaks while standing or even while waving his arms about.
In this way, one displays verbal insolence when in the Saṅgha.
How does one display verbal insolence when in a group?

Here, a certain person, having entered a group, without showing respect and without having asked permission or being requested, speaks Dhamma to the monks who have gone to the monastery, answers questions, speaks while standing, or speaks while waving his arms about.
When he teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhunīs, laymen, or laywomen who have gone to a monastery, answers questions, speaks while standing, or speaks while waving his arms—
thus he displays verbal insolence within a group.
How does one who has entered among the houses display verbal insolence?
Here, someone who has entered among the houses says to a woman or a girl:
"Lady so-and-so of such-and-such a clan, what is there?
Is there rice-gruel? Is there cooked food? Is there solid food?"
"What shall we drink? What shall we eat? What shall we chew? What is there? Or what will you give me?
Thus, having entered among the houses, he displays verbal insolence—this is verbal insolence.
And what is mental insolence?
Here, someone who has gone forth from a noble family does not, in his mind, consider himself equal to one who has gone forth from a noble family;
nor, having gone forth from a family of great wealth, does he, in his mind, consider himself equal to one who has gone forth from a family of great wealth.
Having gone forth from a family of great wealth, he does not, in his mind, consider himself equal to one who has gone forth from a family of great wealth;
being a master of the Suttantas, he does not, in his mind, consider himself equal to a master of the Suttantas;
being a bearer of the Vinaya, he does not...
Not being a preacher of the Dhamma...
not being a forest-dweller...
not being an alms-food eater...
Not being one who wears rag-robes...
not being one who possesses only three robes...
not being one who goes for alms from house to house in regular order...
One who is not a "refuser of food after the meal" does not, by means of his mind, make himself equal to one who is a "refuser of food after the meal";

one who is not a "sitter" does not, by means of his mind, make himself equal to one who is a "sitter"; one who is not a "one who uses whatever seat is offered" does not, by means of his mind, make himself equal to one who is a "one who uses whatever seat is offered."
Being an attainer of the first jhāna, he does not regard himself as equal to one who has attained the first jhāna by way of the mind;
nor [does he do so] regarding the second jhāna… nor the third jhāna…
Not being an attainer of the fourth jhāna… not being an attainer of the attainment of the base of infinite space… not [being an attainer] of the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness…

Being an attainer of the base of nothingness, one does not consider oneself equal to another who is an attainer of the base of nothingness by way of thought; this is mental insolence. Being an attainer of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one does not consider oneself equal to another who is an attainer of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by way of thought;
this is mental insolence.
"He should not train" means he should not train in, practice, conduct himself, behave, or act out of insolence;
he should abandon insolence, dispel it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease.
He should be one who is aloof from insolence, detached, thoroughly detached, emerged from it, escaped from it, and liberated from it; he should dwell with a mind that has transcended its boundaries.
One should not train in insolence.
How does one not engage in contentious speech?
What is contentious speech?
In this case, someone engages in such speech as this:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline... [etc.
...or unravel it if you are able!"
For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Moggallāna, when there is contentious talk, an abundance of talk is to be expected; when there is an abundance of talk, there is agitation; for one who is agitated, there is lack of restraint; for one who lacks restraint, the mind is far from concentration.
How, then, should one not engage in contentious talk?
One should not engage in contentious talk, nor speak it, nor illuminate it, nor utter it; one should abandon contentious talk, dispel it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease.

One should be aloof from contentious talk, abstain from it, refrain from it, have emerged from it, be detached from it, and be liberated from it; one should dwell with a mind for which there is no boundary [of attachment] toward contentious talk. Thus it is said.
How should one not engage in contentious speech?
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"A bhikkhu should not be a quarrelsome disputant."
One should not utter speech that is purposeless;
one should not practice insolence,
and one should not engage in contentious talk.
One should not be led away by flattery,
nor should one, being fully aware, act with deceit;
rather, [one should strive] for life and for wisdom.
"One should not despise another on account of their virtue and observances;
one should not yield to the speaking of falsehood.
By "speaking of falsehood" is meant lying.
Here, someone, having gone to an assembly or a gathering...
[or] for the sake of some trifling material gain, speaks a deliberate lie—
this is called the transgression of lying.
Furthermore, there are three ways in which false speech occurs:

before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak falsely"; while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking falsely"; after having spoken, one thinks, "I have spoken falsely. It is through these three ways that false speech occurs.
Furthermore, there are four ways...
In five ways … in six ways … in seven ways …
False speech occurs in eight ways:
before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak falsely"; while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking falsely"; and after having spoken...
There is the thought, "A falsehood was spoken by me," while setting aside one's view, setting aside one's preference, setting aside one's inclination,
setting aside one's perception, and setting aside one's disposition—
in these eight ways, there is false speech.
"He should not be led away by falsehood":
he should not go toward falsehood, should not be carried away by it, should not be driven by it, should not accumulate it;
he should abandon falsehood, dispel it, bring it to an end, cause it to cease to exist; he should be detached from falsehood, abstain from it, and refrain from it.
Thinking, "May I dwell with a mind that has gone forth, escaped, is liberated, and is detached,
free from the boundaries of the world," one should not be led astray by verbal deception.
Being fully aware, one should not act with deceit.
What is craftiness?
Here, someone is crafty, deceitful toward an assembly; whatever therein is craftiness, being crafty, crookedness, being crooked, scheming, being scheming—this is called craftiness.
Being fully aware, one should not act with deceit.
Being fully aware, one should not practice deceit; one should not produce it, generate it, bring it into being, or cause it to arise.
One should abandon deceit, dispel it, eliminate it, bring it to an end, and lead it to non-existence. One should be one who stands aloof from deceit.
"Abstaining, refraining, having gone out, having emerged, being liberated, and being detached, one should dwell with a mind free from boundaries"—
thus, being clearly comprehending, one should not act with deceit. Furthermore,
one should not despise another on account of life, wisdom, or virtue and observances.
Now, "atha" is a grammatical junction (*padasandhi*)... [etc. ...it is the sequential order of words (*padānupubbatā*): "atha.
Here, someone living a coarse life looks down upon another who lives a refined life.
“But why does this one of abundant livelihood consume everything, namely:
root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, crown-seeds, and fifthly, seed-seeds, with the exertion of an ascetic that is like the peak of a thunderbolt’s wheel?
Thus, because of that coarse way of life, he looks down upon another who lives a refined life.
Here, someone living a refined life looks down upon another who lives a coarse life, thinking:
"Why is this person of little merit and little influence not a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick?
Thus, by means of that refined way of life, he looks down upon another who lives a coarse life.
In this case, someone is endowed with wisdom.
When questioned, he answers the question.
It occurs to him:
“I am endowed with wisdom, but these others are not endowed with wisdom.
He holds others in contempt because of that perfection of wisdom.

Here, someone is endowed with virtue; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
It occurs to him:
"I am endowed with virtue, but these other bhikkhus are immoral and of evil character.
Because of that perfection of virtue, he holds others in contempt.

Here, someone is accomplished in ascetic practices: he may be a forest-dweller, an alms-collector, a wearer of rag-robes, one who possesses only three robes, one who goes on a continuous alms-round, one who refuses food offered after the round, a sitter, or one who accepts whatever seat is offered.
It occurs to him:
"I am accomplished in ascetic practices, but these others are not accomplished in ascetic practices."
Thus, because of that perfection of vows, one looks down upon another. But through life,

wisdom, virtue, and observances, one does not look down on anyone else— whether by a coarse way of life or a refined way of life, or by the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of virtue, or the perfection of vows.
Or one should not despise another, nor look down upon them, nor give rise to conceit because of that,
nor be stiff or arrogant on that account,
thinking, "I am superior by way of life, wisdom, or virtue and observances. Thus, one should not despise another on account of these things.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One should not be led away by the offense of lying;
being fully aware, one should not act with deceit.”
“Then, by life, by wisdom,
or by virtue and observance, one should not despise another.
Having heard much speech, he became enraged.
Whether toward ascetics or toward ordinary people,
one should not respond with harshness;
for the virtuous do not engage in hostility.
"Having heard much speech from ordinary persons among the recluses"—
here, "enraged" (*rusita*) means corrupted, censured, struck, reviled, blamed, or reproached.
"Of the recluses" (*samaṇānam*) refers to whoever have gone forth outside of this [teaching], having entered the life of a wanderer.
"Ordinary people" refers to kshatriyas, brahmins, vaishyas, shudras, householders, renunciants, gods, and humans;
they might revile, abuse, irritate, provoke, harm, injure, vex, harass, strike, or assault one with many words that are undesirable, unpleasant, and disagreeable.
They would cause harm; having heard, having listened to, having grasped, having retained, and having discerned much speech that is undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasant—
having heard such much speech, one becomes provoked by ascetics or by worldlings.
"One does not respond with harshness. "With harshness" means: one should not respond with harshness or roughness;
one should not shout back at one who is shouting, nor get angry at one who is angry, nor engage in counter-quarreling, nor create a quarrel, nor engage in mutual strife.
One should not engage in quarreling, one should not engage in disputing, one should not engage in contention;
one should abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence quarreling, brawling, quarreling, disputing, and contention;

one should be detached from, abstain from, refrain from, have emerged from, escaped from, and be liberated from quarreling, brawling, quarreling, disputing, and contention, and should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
"One should not respond with harshness.
For the noble ones do not act as adversaries.
"The noble ones" (santo) means they are calm because of the calming of lust, anger, delusion, wrath, resentment... and so on... [down to] all unwholesome volitional formations.
Because of being calmed, stilled, tranquillized, extinguished, quenched, departed,
and subsided, one who is calm, stilled, tranquillized, quenched, and subsided is called "peaceful" (*santo*).
"For the noble ones do not create an adversary.
This means that the noble ones do not create, generate, produce, bring forth, or cause to arise an adversary, a rival, an opponent, or an antagonist;
thus, "the noble ones do not create an adversary."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having heard much speech that causes resentment,
whether from recluses or from ordinary people;”
"One should not respond with harshness,
for the virtuous do not act as adversaries.
Having understood this Dhamma,
A bhikkhu should always train himself in what is proximate, being mindful;
knowing that peace is Nibbāna,
he should not be negligent in the teaching of Gotama.
"And having understood this Dhamma":

"This" refers to the Dhamma that has been declared, taught, laid down, established, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and expounded; having understood it, known it, weighed it, scrutinized it, and fully clarified it.
Thus, too, is the meaning of "having understood this Dhamma."
Or alternatively: having understood, known, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest the Dhamma— both the even and the uneven, the path and the non-path,
the blameworthy and the blameless, the inferior and the superior, the dark and the bright,
that which is censured by the wise and that which is praised by the wise.

Likewise, having understood this Dhamma— or alternatively, the practice that is right, the practice that is in accordance [with reality], the practice that is not contrary, the practice that is non-opposing, the practice that is appropriate to the goal,
the practice that is in conformity with the Dhamma, the fulfillment of the precepts, the guarding of the sense doors, and moderation in eating.

Having understood, known, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest the Dhamma— namely, the application of wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path,
and both Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna— he has made it manifest.
"Thus, having understood that Dhamma,
the bhikkhu, always mindful, investigates and trains.
"Investigating" means investigating, scrutinizing, weighing, examining, discerning, and making manifest.

“‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’ …pe… ‘Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation’”— discerning, discriminating, weighing, scrutinizing, clarifying, and making manifest [this],
a bhikkhu is one who discerns.
"Always" means at all times, at every moment,
throughout the entire duration [of life], up until the final stage of existence.
"Mindful" means mindful by way of four causes.
Developing the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body, being mindful … [as above] … he is called “mindful.
He trains: in the three trainings.
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom … [as before] … this is the training in higher wisdom.
One should train by being mindful of these three trainings … [as before] …
"One should train, one should practice, one should practice thoroughly, and having undertaken it, one should conduct oneself"— thus,
a bhikkhu should always train with circumspection and mindfulness.
"Peace" means knowing Nibbāna.
"Knowing that the extinction of lust is peace," and knowing that the extinction of hatred...

the extinction of delusion... and knowing that the extinction of all unwholesome volitional formations is peace—having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest—this is "knowing that extinction is peace."
"In the dispensation of Gotama, one should not be negligent. This means:

in the dispensation of Gotama—the dispensation of the Buddha, the dispensation of the Conqueror, the dispensation of the Tathāgata, the dispensation of the Deva, the dispensation of the Arahant—one should not be negligent.

"One should not be negligent" means that one should be a practitioner of thoroughness, a practitioner of constancy, a practitioner of steadfastness, one who does not live in a state of contraction, one whose desire for wholesome states is not cast aside, and one whose burden is not laid down with respect to wholesome qualities.
“When shall I fulfill the aggregate of virtue that is not yet fulfilled?
…pe… the aggregate of concentration … the aggregate of wisdom that is not yet fulfilled?”
The aggregate of liberation … the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation?

When might I fully understand suffering that has not been fully understood, abandon defilements that have not been abandoned, develop the path that has not been developed, or realize cessation that has not been realized?”

Whatever zeal, effort, exertion, ardor, fortitude, and unyielding persistence there is therein, as well as mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving, resolve, application, and heedfulness regarding wholesome states—
this is how one should not be negligent in the teaching of Gotama.
Thus the Blessed One said.
“Having understood this Dhamma,
a bhikkhu, always mindful, should investigate and train;
knowing that ‘peace’ is Nibbāna, he should practice.”
One should not be negligent in the teaching of Gotama.
For he is the Conqueror, unconquered;
he has seen the Dhamma for himself, beyond mere tradition.
Therefore, indeed, in the teaching of that Blessed One,
one should always train diligently while paying homage.
(Thus spoke the Blessed One.)
"For he is the conqueror, unconquered.
As a conqueror, he is one who has conquered forms, conquered sounds, conquered odors, conquered tastes, conquered tangibles, and conquered mental phenomena;
he is unconquered by any defilements. He has conquered those evil, unwholesome states that lead to corruption and to renewed existence.
Thinking, "In the future, there will be the ripening of suffering, characterized by birth, aging, and death"—
he has indeed overcome it, being unconquered;
he has seen for himself the timeless Dhamma.
"Verified by one’s own direct knowledge" means: he has seen, observed, perceived, and penetrated a dhamma that is personally realized through his own higher knowledge—

not based on hearsay, not based on tradition, not based on rumor, not based on the authority of the Piṭakas, not based on reasoning, not based on logic, not based on reflection on appearances, and not based on approval of a view after pondering it.
He saw the Dhamma as directly evident and not based on tradition.
Therefore, in the teaching of that Blessed One...
"Therefore" means for that reason, for that cause, for that condition, and for that source.
"In the teaching of that Blessed One":

in the teaching of that Blessed One—that is, in the teaching of Gotama, the teaching of the Buddha, the teaching of the Conqueror, the teaching of the Tathāgata, the teaching of the Deva, the teaching of the Arahant;
therefore, "in the teaching of that Blessed One."
"Being diligent, one should always train in paying homage," said the Blessed One.
"Diligent" means one who acts with thorough care...
diligence regarding wholesome states.
Always, at all times ... [and so on] ...
even in the final stage of life.
They pay homage by means of the body, or paying homage by means of speech, or paying homage by means of the mind, through practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
Or paying homage by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma; or paying homage, honoring, respecting, revering, worshipping, and venerating [the Teacher].
"He trains in" refers to the three trainings.
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom … [as before] … this is the training in higher wisdom.
One should train by being mindful of these three trainings … [as before] …
Realizing that which is to be realized, one should train, practice, conduct oneself, act accordingly, and live having undertaken the training.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence... [as above] ...it is a designation for realization, namely, "Bhagavā.
One should always train in paying homage to him with heedfulness.
(Thus said the Blessed One.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For he is the conqueror, unconquered.”
He has seen the Dhamma with his own eyes, which is the treasure of the wise;
therefore, in the teaching of that Blessed One,
one should always train diligently while paying homage.
(Thus said the Blessed One.
The fourteenth exposition, the Tuvaṭaka Sutta, is concluded.
